memory_bridge: Build a five-level lift around the upper stroke: the formal sign 以上 uses On ジョウ; the top platform itself is 上 with Kun うえ; an operator raises a box with 上げる, the box rises with 上がる, and a climber ascends with 上る. The vertical motion is shared, but each full verb keeps agency and nuance clear.

readings.editorial_reason: Promoted because 以上（いじょう）is common, modern, and pedagogically useful.
readings.overlay: Bolt an 以上（いじょう） sign to the upper platform—“at least; above”; the final character supplies On ジョウ.

readings.editorial_reason: Promoted because 上（うえ）is common, modern, and pedagogically useful.
readings.overlay: Stand on the higher stroke and point to the place 上（うえ）, “above”; the standalone native location word fixes Kun うえ.

readings.editorial_reason: Promoted because 上げる（あげる）is common, modern, and pedagogically useful.
readings.overlay: Pull the lift lever and deliberately 上げる（あげる） a box to the top; the complete transitive verb fixes Kun あげる, “to raise.”

readings.editorial_reason: Promoted because 上がる（あがる）is common, modern, and pedagogically useful.
readings.overlay: Release the lever and watch the platform itself 上がる（あがる）; the complete intransitive verb fixes Kun あがる, “to rise.”

readings.editorial_reason: Promoted because 上る（のぼる）is common, modern, and pedagogically useful.
readings.overlay: Finally, have a climber scale the vertical line and 上る（のぼる） to the platform; the complete native verb fixes Kun のぼる, “to ascend.”
